servicesIndustries.name: Wholesale Trade
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Wholesale trade output rose 1.8% month-over-month against the March 2026 reference period, among the strongest monthly service gains — wholesale sales (excluding petroleum and grain) rose 0.6% to $89.3B in April 2026, up 6.3% year-over-year, after $89.0B in March, and Q1 2026 sales ran 1.8% above Q1 2025.12 The machinery and equipment subsector rose 6.5% to $19.5B in March, led by computer and communications equipment, which climbed 17.9% to $5.9B as business investment in capital goods turned over.2

No discrete wholesale tag exists in the project database — the capital-investment pipeline does not track wholesale operations, so the read is sourced from GDP and StatCan wholesale-trade releases rather than project counts.23 Wholesale demand is closely tied to business investment and trade flows; if machinery and equipment turnover holds at the March pace, particularly computer and communications equipment, wholesale sales would continue running above year-ago levels.

servicesIndustries.name: Retail Trade
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Retail trade output declined 0.6% month-over-month against the March 2026 reference period while holding 0.8% above year-ago levels — retail sales rose 0.5% in April 2026, with a preliminary May estimate of +1.0% month-over-month, and e-commerce rose 1.5% in March, holding a 7.1% share of total retail trade.12 Consumer spending has stayed focused on essentials, with discretionary categories more selective, and the divergence between positive sales and negative GDP points to margin and volume shifts within the sector.2

Wholesale-and-retail trade employment fell 35,000 in May, down 1.2% month-over-month and 2.1% year-over-year — trade employment has trended down since October 2025 even as headline sales held positive.3 The project database tracks 97 commercial_mixed records valued at roughly $28.6B, and new grocery-format builds this period include Empire's plan for 70 new stores over three years, Maxi Lévis, Fresh St. Market Richmond, and Nature's Fare Chilliwack.4 If consumer spending stays essentials-weighted, discretionary retail would remain selective while grocery-format expansion adds physical store capacity through 2026.

servicesIndustries.name: Transportation & Warehousing
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Transportation and warehousing output held flat month-over-month but rose 3.1% year-over-year against the March 2026 reference period, the strongest annual gain of any tracked industry — transportation and warehousing employment rose 19,000 in May, up 1.7% month-over-month, on sustained trade and logistics activity.12 Canada's freight and logistics market reached roughly US$116.6B in 2026 on a 4.45% CAGR to 2031, with rail freight near $18.7B; rail handled 11% of export value and about 50% of export volume in 2024.3

The project database tracks 683 transport, transit, and logistics records valued at roughly $54.0B, with 16 first-tracked since June 13 — new entries this period include the OC Transpo electric bus fleet and electrical upgrade in Ontario (Approved), the DSV Innisfil multi-client logistics complex (Complete), and the Ninth Line Road widening (Under Construction).4 Transport Canada estimates $284B is needed for rail upgrades by 2070 against a $2.8B-per-year investment gap, and the $51B Build Communities Strong Fund covers municipal transit; if that allocation disburses, transit and warehousing projects would continue adding to the pipeline.5

servicesIndustries.name: Information & Cultural Industries
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Information and cultural industries output dipped 0.2% month-over-month but rose 3.2% year-over-year against the March 2026 reference period — information, culture, and recreation employment rose 19,000 in May, up 2.3% month-over-month, as telecom and content investment offset losses elsewhere in the bucket.12 The CRTC set online-broadcaster contribution at 15% of revenue and traditional broadcasters at 25% in May 2026, stabilizing Canadian and Indigenous content funding above $2B, paired with a federal commitment of $600M per year to the cultural sector.3

The project database tracks 95 telecom records valued at roughly $88.7B, overlapping the data-centre and fibre buildout tagged under NAICS 54 — the Canada Media Fund set a $359M program budget for 2026-27, while the past year saw hundreds of media-industry layoffs, with closures outpacing launches in community news.34 If the CRTC framework and the $600M-per-year cultural commitment hold, content funding would stay above $2B, and telecom and data-centre capex would continue overlapping with professional-services infrastructure.4

servicesIndustries.name: Finance & Insurance
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Finance and insurance output held flat month-over-month but rose 3.6% year-over-year against the March 2026 reference period, among the strongest service annual readings — all six major banks beat estimates in Q2 2026, and all except CIBC raised dividends.12 National Bank reported $3.23 adjusted EPS against a $3.14 consensus, and CIBC's Q1 adjusted figure of $2.76 topped a $2.40 expectation; Canadian bank stocks rose 16% year-to-date in 2026 against the TSX Composite's 8%.2

No discrete finance project tag exists in the database, so the read is sourced from earnings and equity data rather than capital records — BMO has cut more than 670 jobs since Q3 2025, booking $202M in pre-tax severance in Q1, while property and casualty insurers face auto-claims inflation and softening commercial lines.23 Finance demand tracks interest rates and asset prices; if credit conditions and equity valuations hold, bank earnings momentum would persist while cost actions continue to compress headcount.

servicesIndustries.name: Real Estate & Rental/Leasing
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Real estate and rental/leasing output rose 0.1% month-over-month and 1.8% year-over-year against the March 2026 reference period — CBRE projects commercial real estate investment could rise to roughly $56B in 2026, up 8% from $47B in 2025 and the third-highest on record.12 National office vacancy was 13.6% in Q1 2026, down about one percentage point year-over-year, as return-to-office mandates supported Class A demand while older buildings faced pressure.2

No discrete real-estate tag exists in the database; residential and commercial development is captured under construction (NAICS 23) — the new Forêt Forest Hill tower in Ontario advanced to Under Construction with Canderel, and lumber, a residential development input, rose 6.4% over the month.23 Real estate activity tracks mortgage rates, immigration, and housing policy; if return-to-office demand and investment momentum continue, Class A office and commercial transaction volumes would stay elevated relative to 2025.

servicesIndustries.name: Professional, Scientific & Technical Services
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Professional, scientific and technical services output declined 0.2% month-over-month and 0.4% year-over-year against the March 2026 reference period, after 2.2% growth in 2024 — firms are redirecting investment toward AI capacity even as headline GDP stays near flat.12 A federal call for 100MW-plus sovereign AI data centres ran January 15 to February 15, 2026, and Microsoft committed C$19B to Canadian AI and cloud in December 2025, with more than C$7.5B landing within two years and an Ontario tranche supporting 1,250 jobs.2

No discrete professional-services project tag exists; data-centre capex overlaps telecom, utilities, and construction — five hyperscale data centres are operating across BC, Ontario, Quebec, and New Brunswick, with 96 more announced or under construction at roughly $10M per MW plus more than $30M per MW of compute.23 About 19% of the West and North workforce is over 55 with rising retirements through 2026; if the sovereign-AI data-centre commitments proceed, professional-services demand tied to systems design and R&D would draw on those 96 announced facilities.3

servicesIndustries.name: Management of Companies & Enterprises
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Management of companies and enterprises output fell 1.3% month-over-month and 22.7% year-over-year against the March 2026 reference period, the largest GDP swing of any industry in the series — this bucket captures holding companies and head-office functions, where large annual moves typically reflect intercompany reclassification rather than operating-economy activity.1 No significant capital-project developments were found for the sector this period.12

No discrete project tag exists for this holding-company and head-office bucket, so the narrative is sourced from GDP only — the -22.7% reading is the deepest annual move in the industry GDP series but is consistent with reclassification volatility, not a change in underlying operating output.12 If the reclassification effect normalizes, the reported NAICS 55 figure would revert toward the underlying operating trend; no capital projects are tied to this bucket.

The project database tracks 272 environment records valued at roughly $2.6B, capturing the remediation and cleanup pipeline overlapping this NAICS — federal remediation funding and the $5.03B Top 25 list underpin the bucket despite the slightly negative annual GDP reading.23 Remediation demand tracks government environmental budgets; if FCSAP Phase V and provincial remediation programs disburse on schedule, the 272-record pipeline would continue advancing through 2030.3

servicesIndustries.name: Educational Services
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Educational services output held flat month-over-month but fell 2.8% year-over-year against the March 2026 reference period, among the weaker annual service readings — international-student declines and a tuition freeze have pressured operating revenue, with Ontario's college sector facing up to a $1.5B deficit by 2027-28.12 Universities and colleges are eligible for the federal Provincial-Territorial infrastructure stream at $17.2B over ten years, with 23 Direct Delivery projects including TMU School of Medicine in Brampton and Inuit Nunangat University.2

The project database tracks 151 education records valued at roughly $7.3B, with one first-tracked since June 13 — BC committed $4.4B in post-secondary capital over three years, including an SFU Surrey medical school, while $50M was directed to an Inuit-led university in Arviat, Nunavut.23 Education capital tracks government budgets and demographics; if the federal infrastructure stream and BC's $4.4B post-secondary capital disburse, education construction would continue even as operating GDP stays soft.3

servicesIndustries.name: Health Care & Social Assistance
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Health care and social assistance output held flat month-over-month and rose 2.0% year-over-year against the March 2026 reference period, supported by demographics and multi-year provincial hospital programs — Ontario plans roughly $64B in health infrastructure over ten years, covering 50 hospital projects and 3,000 new beds.12 UHN Toronto Western's 15-storey surgical tower exceeds $750M with 82 rooms, the Peter Gilgan Mississauga Hospital is more than 45% excavated, and Royal Columbian Phase 2 in BC opened in May 2026.2

The project database tracks 222 healthcare records valued at roughly $51.1B, with 8 first-tracked since June 13 — the Saskatchewan Health Authority posted 6 Saskatoon roles this week, 6.0 times its tracked average, and the new Tumbler Ridge school and health centre in BC carries a $200M value.34 Health-sector demand tracks population aging and provincial budgets; if provincial health-infrastructure plans proceed on schedule, the 222-record pipeline would continue expanding through the decade.4

servicesIndustries.name: Accommodation & Food Services
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Accommodation and food services output fell 0.4% month-over-month but ran 0.5% above year-ago levels against the March 2026 reference period — accommodation and food employment rose 17,000 in May, up 1.5% month-over-month, against a 3.8% job-vacancy rate recorded in 2024, roughly 18,230 unfilled positions versus 3.1% across all industries.12 Tourism visitor spending is forecast at $140.9B in 2026, up 6% from 2025 on domestic, US, and overseas demand, growing faster than the wider economy.2

No discrete accommodation and food tag exists; activity is captured within the tourism_culture project bucket under NAICS 71 — the sector employs roughly 2.1 million people, and Ontario accommodation and food employed 426,700 in 2023, 37.8% of the national sector.23 Demand tracks tourism, business travel, and consumer spending; if the projected 6% tourism-spending growth materializes, accommodation and food labour demand would stay elevated against an already-tight vacancy rate.3

servicesIndustries.name: Public Administration
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Public administration output rose 0.4% month-over-month and 1.1% year-over-year against the March 2026 reference period — the 2026-27 Main Estimates total $502.8B in budgetary spending, $230.4B voted and $272.4B statutory, with transfer payments at 59.8% or $300.5B.12 The Spring Economic Update sets priorities of $25B for housing, $30B for defence, $115B for infrastructure, and $110B for productivity over five years, alongside $60B in spending reductions.2

The project database tracks 286 government and defence records valued at roughly $146.2B, with 10 first-tracked since June 13 — defence procurement this period includes the $39B Canada Submarine Fleet Replacement (Proposed), the $2.5B Far North Early Warning Arctic Radar in NT, and the $2.5B Canadian Naval Radar in NS.23 Public-administration capital tracks government budgets and policy priorities; if the submarine and Arctic-radar programs advance from Proposed status, the $146.2B pipeline would continue expanding through the procurement cycle.3
